20.​Add after paragraph 64 and renumber (London - Camden) 
 
Britain’s military has been exposed as decades behind the major powers by the wars 
in the Ukraine and the Middle East. As militarism sweeps Europe, its numbers 
continue to fall as its materiel dilapidates and becomes obsolete. It has long been 
merely a component part of the US’s European Front and relies on the rest of NATO 
for arms manufacturing and operational cohesion. For instance, Britain lacks a 
ground-based missile defence system and is now scrambling to buy one from a 
French company. Economic and political weaknesses are thus directly translated into 
military terms. Meanwhile, the British capitalists maintain delusions of global 
influence fostered by the post-war order. Their “strategy” has become 
impressionistic, improvising alliances and priorities to avoid confronting their greatly 
diminished global role. They begrudge Trump’s strategy of having his European 
lackeys increase military spending to focus on opposing Russia. British ships 
continue to patrol the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific, with the Iran War exposing 
how pointless this is, while vast sums are wasted on vanity projects like leasing US 
nuclear weapons. British imperialism is an overstretched and unreliable ally, to the US 
or anyone else. It is organically unable to recognise its own decline and this becomes 
a factor accelerating it. 
 
CC recommendation: Reject in favour of amendment 21 
 
21.​Add after paragraph 68 and renumber (Central Committee) 
 
Britain’s military expenditure is already very high – it has the sixth largest defence 
budget in the world. However, a growing proportion of this is spent on nuclear 
weapons and military intelligence, which are heavily integrated with the US military. In 
terms of troops and conventional weaponry, the British military is in a parlous state 
after decades of underinvestment and cutbacks. 
 
Military chiefs in Britain and allied countries, most vocally the USA, are demanding 
huge increases in defence spending to prevent Britain slipping into an even weaker 
position on a conflict-ridden world stage. But politicians are struggling to squeeze the 
money out of a crisis-ridden capitalist system. The only way to do so would be huge 
attacks on the working class, provoking class struggle. Starmer is trying to balance 
between these opposing pressures, satisfying neither and paving the way for a 
sharpening of this contradiction. 
 
CC recommendation: Accept​
